<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
Given a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ of characteristic $p$ (where $p=0$ is allowed), given $n$ a positive integer not divisible by $p$, and $\xi$ an $n$th root of unity in $\mathbb{F}_q$, we define $$Q_n(x)=\prod_{s=1}^n\left (x-\xi^s\right)$$ as the $n$-cyclotomic polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_q$, which has degree equal to $\varphi(n)$, where $\varphi$ is Euler’s function.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- defn-2: body_md -->
Let $n$ be a positive integer, and $b$ an integer coprime to $n$. The smallest positive integer $k$ such that $n\mid(b^k-1),$ which is equivalent to $b^k\equiv 1\pmod{n},$ is called the multiplicative order of $b$ modulo $n$ and is denoted by $ord_n(b)=k$.
<!-- end defn-2 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
Given a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, a positive integer $n$ such that $\gcd(q,n)=1$, and $d=ord_n(q)$, then $Q_n(x)$ factors into exactly $\varphi(n)/d$ distinct polynomials in $\mathbb{F}_q[x]$, all of degree $d$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field, $n$ a prime distinct from $p$ such that $q = p^k$ and $ord_n(q) = n - 1$. Then $Q_n(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_q[x]$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Since $n$ is prime and distinct from $p$, then $\gcd(n,q)=1$. By the previous theorem, $Q_n(x)$ factors into $\varphi(n)/ord_n(q)$ polynomials, but $\varphi(n)=n-1$ and $ord_n(q)=n-1$ by assumption, so $\varphi(n)/ord_n(q)=1$ and $Q_n(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_q[x]$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
It is also a sufficient condition; that is, given a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $n > 2$ such that $x^n - 1 = (x - 1) \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} x^j$ and has no other factors, then $n$ is prime, $\gcd(n, q) = 1$, and $ord_n(q) = n - 1$.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We have already shown that if $n$ is composite, then $x^n - 1$ has more than two factors; therefore, if $x^n - 1$ has exactly two factors, $n$ is prime.

    If we assume that $\gcd(n,q) \not=  1$, then $\gcd(n,q)=n$ (since $n$ is prime); thus, $q=n^k$ and the characteristic of $\mathbb{F}_q$ is $n$. This implies that $x^n-1=(x-1)^n$, which always has more than two factors if $n>2$, which cannot be the case. Therefore, $\gcd(n,q)=1$.

    Finally, suppose that $ord_n(q) \neq n-1$ and let $ord_n(q) = d$. Since $n$ is prime, the multiplicative group of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ has $n-1$ elements, and by Lagrange’s theorem, the order $d$ must divide $n-1$. Since $n$ is prime, $Q_n(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}x^j$, and we know that it factors into $\varphi(n)/d$ distinct factors; since $d<n-1$, $\varphi(n)/d=(n-1)/d\geq 2$. Therefore, $x^n-1$ has at least three factors, which is impossible by assumption. Thus, $ord_n(q) = n-1$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
In a finite field of order $q$, if for our signature we choose a ma\-trix size $n$ such that $n > 2$ is prime, $\gcd(n, q) = 1$, and $ord_n(q) = n - 1$, the probability $P$ that a circulant matrix is invertible is
    
    $$P = \frac {(q^1-1)(q^{n-1}-1)}{q^n}=\frac{q-1}{q}-\frac{q-1}{q^n},$$
    
    so for enough large values of $n$ that satisfy the required conditions, this probability will be less than $(q-1)/q$, an efficient value for digital signatures.
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
Suppose that the signature scheme $S$ is secure and that the hash function $H$ is collision-resistant. Then the associated signature $\text{S'}=(G,S',V')$, as defined above, is secure.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
